standard.title: Binary representation
standard.description: Explore how data can be represented by off and on states (zeros and ones in binary)
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how digital systems represent all data using numbers (AC9TDI6K03). They understand that text and other data types are stored as numbers. They have not yet explored how numbers themselves are represented in a digital system — the binary (on/off) basis of all digital data.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore how on/off states in digital circuits can represent zeros and ones, and how binary is the fundamental representation underlying all digital data.

nodes.label: On/off states represent zero and one
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that an on/off state in a digital circuit represents the digits one and zero
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate or explain that a two-state system (on/off, yes/no, long/short) can represent 1 and 0; connect this to how digital systems store data at the physical level
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate that an on/off state in a circuit represents 1 and 0; recognise that yes/no questions, Morse code dashes and dots, and circuit states all use the same two-state principle; explain that digital systems use billions of these switches to store complex data
wider: Create a binary representation of a word or phrase (e.g. the name of a local Country/Place in a First Nations language) using beads, switches or symbols — demonstrating that any two-state medium can encode binary data
Investigate how punch cards or early telegraph systems used physical two-state mechanisms to encode information before electronic computers existed

response_modes.reason: Students often struggle to see that binary is an abstract principle, not a specific technology. Seeing the same on/off structure in circuits, Morse code, beads, and yes/no questions helps students abstract the principle: any two distinguishable states can encode 0 and 1.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The collaborative binary banner/bead activity with First Nations language names (from the elaboration) is genuinely rich — it grounds an abstract representation concept in a physical, culturally meaningful artifact that also serves as an Acknowledgement of Country.
success_criteria: Explains that an on/off state represents 1 and 0 in a digital system
Gives at least one example of a two-state system representing binary data
nodes.hinge_reason: The on/off state = 0/1 concept is definitionally required for N2 — without it, the integration of numeric representation (K03) with physical storage cannot proceed. N2's chain (data → number → binary → physical state) collapses at the last step.

nodes.label: Binary connects numeric representation to physical storage
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how binary connects the numeric representation of data (from AC9TDI6K03) to the physical on/off states in a digital system
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that numbers stored in a digital system are ultimately represented as sequences of on/off states — each digit (0 or 1) corresponds to one switch state
nodes.typical_width: Trace the connection from data (e.g. the letter 'A') → number (65 in ASCII) → binary sequence (01000001) → physical on/off states; explain each step in the chain
wider: Represent a short word in binary using a provided encoding table; explain that the digital system performs this translation billions of times per second
Investigate how the number of binary digits (bits) limits how many different values can be stored — 1 bit = 2 values, 2 bits = 4 values, 8 bits = 256 values

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the data-as-numbers understanding from K03 with the binary/on-off understanding from K04 node 1. Tracing the full chain (data → number → binary → physical state) is the integration act — students who cannot connect these steps have two disconnected facts rather than a system understanding.

success_criteria: Connects the idea that data is stored as numbers to the idea that numbers are stored as binary sequences
Can describe the on/off state interpretation of at least one binary digit
